articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent less than a third of collected funds. Commissioners blame supply chains. Engineers blame commissioners. Residents blame everyone.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.2 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but spent only $14.8 million on actual projects
Internal documents show at least 12 shovel-ready projects delayed by what engineers describe as 'decision paralysis' at the commission level
Flooding complaints in fee-paying areas have increased 34% since the program launched
articles.body:
The drainage ditch behind Sandra Mitchum's house on Doris Drive hasn't been cleaned in four years. She knows because she marks the date on her kitchen calendar every time a county truck shows up. The last entry: March 2022.

"They came out here three times before that election asking me to vote yes," Mitchum said, standing in her carport while water pooled at the edge of her driveway. A Tuesday afternoon storm had dropped two inches in an hour. "Said they needed the money to fix the flooding. I voted yes. My neighbors voted yes. Where's the money?"

It's a reasonable question. In November 2023, Escambia County voters approved a dedicated stormwater fee by a 58-42 margin. The fee—$4.50 per month for single-family homes, scaled rates for commercial properties—was projected to generate $15 to $17 million annually for drainage improvements, flood mitigation and infrastructure maintenance.

Two and a half years later, the county has collected $47.2 million. It has spent $14.8 million.

The remaining $32.4 million sits in a dedicated fund, accruing interest while residents like Mitchum watch water rise in their yards.

The spending gap

County budget documents obtained through a public records request show a consistent pattern since the fee took effect in January 2024. Collections have exceeded projections every quarter. Expenditures have fallen short every quarter.

In fiscal year 2024, the county collected $16.3 million and spent $8.1 million. In fiscal year 2025, it collected $17.4 million and spent $6.7 million. Through the first seven months of fiscal year 2026, it has collected $13.5 million and spent just $3.2 million.

The math is simple. The explanations are not.

"We've dealt with unprecedented supply chain challenges," Commissioner Jeff Bergosh said at an April budget workshop. "Pipe materials, concrete, specialized equipment—everything costs more and takes longer to get. We're being responsible stewards of taxpayer money by not overpaying."

That explanation doesn't satisfy Matt Richardson, a licensed civil engineer who spent 18 years with the county's public works department before retiring in 2024. Richardson, who helped design the stormwater fee program, said supply chain issues account for perhaps 15% of the delay.

"The materials excuse was valid in 2022, maybe early 2023," Richardson said. "It's not valid now. Lead times on corrugated pipe are back to eight weeks. Concrete is available. The problem is they can't agree on which projects to prioritize, so nothing moves."

Twelve projects in limbo

Internal memos from the county's engineering division tell a more complicated story than commissioners have offered publicly.

A December 2025 memo from Engineering Director Paula Steadham to County Administrator Wes Moreno identified 12 projects that had completed design, secured permits and were "ready for bid advertisement." Total estimated cost: $22.7 million. Status: awaiting commission direction.

"These projects have been presented to the board three times," Steadham wrote. "Each presentation has resulted in requests for additional information, alternative designs or reconsideration of priority rankings. Staff requires clear direction to proceed."

The projects range from a $1.2 million culvert replacement on Navy Boulevard to a $6.4 million regional detention pond near the Brownsville community. Some have been in the design phase since 2021.

Commissioner Lumon May, whose District 3 includes several of the delayed projects, said the board isn't ignoring the backlog.

"We have an obligation to make sure we're spending this money right," May said. "These are 30-year infrastructure decisions. I'm not going to rubber-stamp something because there's pressure to spend."

But Richardson and other former county engineers argue the constant review cycles amount to paralysis.

"Every time a project comes to the board, somebody wants to know if we considered a different location, or a bigger pipe, or a different contractor," Richardson said. "Those are legitimate questions—the first time. By the third or fourth time, you're just running out the clock."

Flooding gets worse

While the money accumulates, the water keeps rising.

Data from the county's 311 system shows flooding-related complaints have increased 34% in fee-paying areas since the stormwater program launched. In 2023, the county logged 1,847 drainage complaints. In 2025, it logged 2,476.

The Brownsville neighborhood, where the $6.4 million detention pond remains on hold, accounted for 312 complaints last year. Myrtle Grove logged 287. Warrington: 203.

Residents in those communities have organized. A group calling itself "We Paid, Now Drain" has shown up to the last four commission meetings, wearing matching yellow t-shirts and carrying signs with messages like "$47 Million Reasons to Act" and "Stop Studying, Start Digging."

"We did everything they asked," said Marcus Webb, a Brownsville resident who has led the group. "We voted for the fee. We're paying the fee. We're not asking for anything free. We're asking them to spend our money on what they promised to spend it on."

Webb's house flooded in September 2025 during what the National Weather Service classified as a 25-year rain event. He said his insurance claim was denied because flood damage wasn't covered under his standard homeowner's policy.

"They told us this fee would reduce flooding," Webb said. "It hasn't reduced anything. My floors are still warped."

The money trail

Where has the $14.8 million gone?

According to county expenditure reports, approximately $6.2 million has funded actual construction projects—pipe replacements, ditch maintenance, outfall repairs. Another $4.1 million has gone to engineering design and permitting work. The remaining $4.5 million covers program administration, equipment purchases and "contingency allocations."

That last category drew scrutiny at a March commission meeting when resident Tom Farley asked for specifics during public comment.

"What's a contingency allocation?" Farley asked. "Is that a slush fund?"

Moreno, the county administrator, explained that contingency funds are held against potential cost overruns on active projects. When projects come in under budget, contingency funds return to the general stormwater balance.

"It's standard practice," Moreno said. "We're not hiding anything."

Perhaps not hiding. But not exactly advertising either. The county's stormwater program website, last updated in August 2025, lists the fee amount, the rationale and a general description of planned improvements. It does not list specific projects, timelines, budgets or expenditures.

Moreno said a more detailed dashboard is "in development."

What comes next

Commissioner Doug Underhill, who opposed the original stormwater fee, has called for an independent audit of the program.

"We sold voters on a specific promise," Underhill said. "Three years later, the promise is mostly unfulfilled. At minimum, we owe them a full accounting of what happened to their money."

No other commissioner has publicly backed the audit proposal. It has not been placed on an agenda.

Meanwhile, hurricane season opens in two weeks. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration is forecasting an above-average year, with 17 to 20 named storms expected.

Back on Doris Drive, Sandra Mitchum has stopped waiting for the county truck. She hired a private contractor to clear her ditch last month. Cost: $1,800.

"I'm 67 years old," she said. "I don't have time to wait for them to figure it out."

She pulled out her kitchen calendar and flipped to the page where she tracks county maintenance visits. The March 2022 entry sat alone on the grid, a small blue checkmark fading with age.

"Maybe I'll mark when I paid to do it myself," she said. "At least that's a date that means something."

articles.label: Development & Infrastructure
articles.headline: The Last Hold-Outs of West Cervantes
articles.dek: A proposed mixed-use development would reshape six blocks near Bayview Park. But three property owners aren't selling, and the developer's timeline is slipping.
brief: Tampa-based Coastal Urban Partners has acquired 23 of 26 parcels needed for a $180 million mixed-use project on West Cervantes Street
Three property owners—including a 40-year barbershop and a family holding company—have refused multiple buyout offers
The developer's original groundbreaking target of Q3 2026 is now unlikely, with financing contingencies tied to full site control
articles.body:
The chairs inside Ray's Classic Cuts haven't moved in 40 years. Four stations, green vinyl, cracked in the same places they cracked in the Reagan administration. Ray Davenport bought the building at 1847 West Cervantes Street in 1986 for $31,000. Last month, a man in a gray suit offered him $1.2 million for it.

Davenport said no.

"I told him the same thing I told the last three," Davenport said, sweeping hair from the linoleum floor on a Tuesday afternoon. "This isn't a number problem. I don't want to sell."

Davenport's barbershop sits near the center of a six-block stretch of West Cervantes that Tampa-based Coastal Urban Partners wants to transform into The Bayview Collective—a 340-unit residential complex with ground-floor retail, a public plaza and a 400-space parking structure. The project would be the largest private development in Pensacola's Westside in more than two decades.

But three property owners are holding out. And the developer's timeline is starting to buckle.

The Holdouts

Coastal Urban has acquired 23 of the 26 parcels it needs to assemble the full project site. The company has spent approximately $14.7 million on acquisitions since late 2024, according to Escambia County property records.

Three properties remain outside its control:

Davenport's barbershop. A single-family home at 1823 West Cervantes owned by the Tran Family Trust. And a small commercial building at the corner of Cervantes and N Street, owned by a Jacksonville-based LLC called Gulfside Holdings.

Representatives for the Tran Family Trust did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The property has been in the family since 1971 and currently sits vacant, its windows boarded.

Gulfside Holdings acquired its parcel in 2019 for $285,000. The company's registered agent, Kenneth Mallory, declined to discuss the property in detail but confirmed Coastal Urban has made "several offers."

"We're evaluating our options," Mallory said by phone. "That's all I can say."

The Developer's Bind

Coastal Urban Partners has developed mixed-use projects in Tampa, St. Petersburg and Jacksonville. The Bayview Collective would be its first in the Panhandle.

Company president David Forsythe presented the project to the Pensacola City Council's development committee in February, describing it as a "catalytic investment" in a neighborhood that has seen little private capital in decades.

"West Cervantes has been overlooked for too long," Forsythe said at the meeting. "We see it as one of the last great opportunities in urban Pensacola."

But the project's financing is contingent on full site control—a standard requirement for developments of this scale. Coastal Urban's primary lender, a regional bank based in Birmingham, has set a deadline of September 1 for the company to demonstrate it has acquired or secured options on all 26 parcels.

The original groundbreaking was slated for Q3 2026. That timeline now appears unlikely.

Forsythe declined to comment for this article. A company spokesperson provided a written statement: "We remain committed to The Bayview Collective and continue productive conversations with all stakeholders. We're confident in the project's future."

'They Want Us Gone'

The stretch of West Cervantes between N Street and DeVilliers has never been Pensacola's showcase corridor. Dollar stores. A pawn shop. Two bail bondsmen. A church that meets in what used to be a dry cleaner. The kind of block people drive through, not to.

But for those who have been here for decades, the neighborhood's lack of reinvestment is also what made it affordable.

Ray Davenport raised three children in the apartment above his barbershop. Two of them still live within a mile of here. His clientele—working men, mostly Black, mostly from the Westside—have followed him through four decades. Some bring their grandsons now.

"They tell me I can just relocate," Davenport said. "Where? Where am I supposed to go that my customers can find me? That I can afford?"

He's 71 years old. He still cuts hair five days a week.

"This is my retirement plan," he said, gesturing at the walls. "This building. This corner. They want us gone so they can build something shiny. But I'm not gone yet."

Legal Options, Limited

Florida law permits the use of eminent domain for certain private developments deemed to serve a public purpose, but the threshold is high and the process lengthy. Pensacola officials have not indicated any intention to pursue condemnation on behalf of Coastal Urban.

City Council member Marcus DeWitt, whose district includes the project area, said he supports the development but would not support forced acquisition.

"Private property rights matter," DeWitt said. "If the developer can't reach an agreement with these owners, that's between them. The city isn't going to step in and force anyone out of their home or business."

Without eminent domain, Coastal Urban's options are limited: continue negotiating, redesign the project to work around the holdout parcels, or walk away.

Redesigning the project would likely reduce its unit count and could jeopardize the financing. Walking away would mean writing off nearly $15 million in acquisitions.

Neither option is attractive.

Waiting

On a recent Thursday evening, the sun dropped behind the trees at Bayview Park, two blocks south of Davenport's barbershop. A few kids played basketball on the public courts. An older man fished from the seawall, his line disappearing into the brown water of Bayou Texar.

The Bayview Collective's renderings show a rooftop bar with a view of this same water. A dog park. A coffee shop with outdoor seating. The kind of place that gets featured in lifestyle magazines and regional best-of lists.

It may still happen. But not soon. And not without the holdouts agreeing to something they've so far refused.

Ray Davenport closed his shop at 6 p.m. and locked the door. The OPEN sign in the window flickered off. He climbed the stairs to his apartment, same as he has for 40 years.

The developers can wait.

So can he.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: NAS Pensacola's New Flight Pattern Brings More Noise to East Hill
articles.dek: A training route adjustment in March has doubled low-altitude passes over residential neighborhoods. The Navy says it's temporary. Residents have heard that before.
brief: Naval Air Station Pensacola shifted training flight patterns in March, routing more T-6 Texan II aircraft over East Hill and East Pensacola Heights
Residents report 40-60 low-altitude passes daily, up from roughly 20 before the change, with some flights occurring as early as 6:30 a.m.
Navy officials call the adjustment temporary while runway maintenance continues, but have not provided an end date
articles.body:
The T-6 Texan II banked hard over 12th Avenue at 7:14 on a Tuesday morning, low enough that Martha Griggs could see the rivets on its belly. She was standing in her backyard with a coffee cup she'd stopped drinking from. The turboprop roar swallowed whatever her neighbor was trying to say across the fence.

"That's the fourth one since I came outside," Griggs said. "And I've only been out here twenty minutes."

Since March, residents of East Hill and East Pensacola Heights have watched Naval Air Station Pensacola's training aircraft multiply overhead. What was once a manageable presence—maybe 15 to 20 passes on a busy day—has become something closer to constant. Neighbors who've tracked the flights say they're now counting 40, 50, sometimes 60 daily.

The Navy confirms a route adjustment took effect March 11. Runway 8/26 at NAS Pensacola entered a maintenance phase that required shifting primary training operations to Runway 17/35. That shift pushed the standard flight pattern east, directly over some of the city's oldest residential neighborhoods.

"Training requirements haven't changed," said Lt. Cmdr. Rachel Espinoza, a public affairs officer for Naval Air Training Command. "What's changed is where those training flights are most concentrated geographically."

Espinoza described the adjustment as temporary. She could not provide a timeline for when Runway 8/26 would return to full operation.

Measuring the noise

The Navy does not maintain public noise monitors over East Hill. The closest official measurement station sits near the base's western perimeter, oriented toward Warrington.

Residents have started keeping their own records. Tom Brennan, a retired acoustic engineer who lives on Gadsden Street, has been running a decibel meter from his front porch since April 1. His logs show peak readings between 78 and 89 decibels during low passes—comparable to a garbage disposal or a gas lawn mower at close range.

"It's not that any single flight is unbearable," Brennan said. "It's the accumulation. Your nervous system doesn't get to reset."

The flights typically begin around 6:30 a.m. and continue until early evening, with a brief reduction during lunch hours. Weekends bring fewer passes but not silence.

NAS Pensacola's Air Installation Compatible Use Zone study, last updated in 2019, designated much of East Hill as falling within acceptable noise exposure limits. That study assumed flight patterns that no longer apply.

'Temporary' has a history here

Longtime residents recall similar assurances during previous pattern shifts. In 2017, runway work pushed training flights over the same neighborhoods for what the Navy initially described as a six-week adjustment. It lasted four months.

Pensacola City Council member Tennie White, whose District 6 includes East Hill, said her office has received more than 200 noise complaints since March. She's requested a meeting with base leadership.

"I'm not anti-Navy. Nobody in this city is," White said. "But 'temporary' needs to mean something. And if it can't mean something, then we need to talk about mitigation."

White has asked the Navy to provide weekly updates on runway maintenance progress and to consider voluntary quiet hours before 7 a.m.

Espinoza said the base would take the requests under advisement but noted that training schedules are dictated by curriculum requirements and weather windows.

The math of military aviation

NAS Pensacola is home to the Chief of Naval Air Training's primary flight instruction. Student aviators and flight officers cycle through in cohorts, each requiring a set number of flight hours before advancing. The T-6 Texan II is the workhorse of that system—a single-engine turboprop trainer that's loud by design.

"You can't make these aircraft quiet," said Dr. David Nguyen, an aerospace engineering professor at the University of West Florida who has consulted on military noise studies. "You can route them differently. That's about it."

Nguyen noted that noise complaints near military installations have increased nationally over the past decade, driven partly by residential development creeping closer to base perimeters. East Hill doesn't fit that pattern—these neighborhoods predate the air station—but the dynamic is similar. The tension between mission and community isn't new. It just gets louder sometimes.

Living with it

Back on 12th Avenue, Martha Griggs has started wearing noise-canceling headphones while gardening. She bought them in April. She doesn't like how they feel.

"I moved here in 1994," she said. "I knew the base was there. I'm not naive. But this is different. This is relentless."

Her neighbor, who asked not to be named because he works as a contractor on base, said he's given up trying to have phone calls from his backyard.

"I support the mission," he said. "I also support being able to hear myself think."

The next T-6 came over at 7:31. Then another at 7:38. Griggs didn't look up.
